name: The Greater Fool Theory
statement: An overpriced asset can still be profitably bought if a "greater fool" is later willing to pay an even higher price for it.
statementAccent: a "greater fool" is later willing to pay an even higher price
meaning: The greater fool theory says that in a speculative market, an investor can profit from buying an asset priced above its intrinsic value, as long as someone else — the "greater fool" — will buy it later at a still-higher price. Profit depends not on fundamentals but on finding a buyer more optimistic, or less informed, than oneself. The chain breaks when no new buyers will pay more, and prices collapse toward fundamental value.
mechanism: Rising prices attract media attention and stories of early profits, drawing new buyers through herd behaviour and fear of missing out, pushing prices further from intrinsic value. This self-reinforcing cycle continues only as long as fresh buyers keep entering; once they cannot be found or belief in further gains collapses, a sell-off drives prices sharply down, leaving the last buyers with losses.

examples.text: Tulip mania in the 1630s Netherlands, where bulb prices rose to extraordinary levels before collapsing in 1637, is commonly cited as an early illustration of greater-fool dynamics.
During the late-1990s dot-com bubble, investors bought shares in internet companies with no profits, betting others would buy at higher prices, until the NASDAQ crashed from 2000.

Cryptocurrencies are frequently cited as the theory in action, with several Nobel laureate economists arguing many have no intrinsic value, making price gains dependent purely on finding later buyers.

whyItMatters: It is a widely used framework in finance and behavioural economics for explaining asset-price bubbles and warning investors that price momentum alone is not evidence of underlying value.
limits: The theory does not predict when a bubble will burst or who will be left holding the asset, and it can be applied retroactively to almost any price decline, making it more a descriptive heuristic than a testable model. It also risks conflating legitimate rising valuations, justified by improving fundamentals, with pure speculation.
misreadings: It is sometimes misread as implying all rising asset prices are irrational bubbles; the theory specifically describes cases where the buyer knowingly pays above perceived intrinsic value in anticipation of resale, not ordinary appreciation grounded in fundamentals.
origin: The term describes a long-recognised speculative pattern rather than a single scholarly theory; it is not attributed to one named originator or exact coinage date, though the dynamic has been discussed in finance writing for over a century.

sources.text: Greater fool theory, Wikipedia. — the definition, psychological mechanism, and examples including tulip mania and cryptocurrency.
"Greater Fool Theory," Corporate Finance Institute. — the definition and mechanism of profiting by reselling overvalued assets to a less-informed buyer.
